newsitem.title: BOSNIA: West cranks up pressure on Bosnian Serb hardliners.
newsitem.headline: West cranks up pressure on Bosnian Serb hardliners.

text.p: Western governments, promoting a tougher policy on indicted war criminals, are turning up the diplomatic heat on hardline Bosnian Serb leaders loyal to wartime leader Radovan Karadzic.

Senior envoys from the United States and European powers have warned Serb ultra-nationalists this month that the West will not be intimidated by revenge attacks over a NATO raid on Serbs wanted for war atrocities.

U.S. Assistant Secretary of State John Shattuck called the retaliatory violence "intolerable" during a weekend visit to Bosnia. He told reporters that the war crimes issue was "the top priority on our agenda".

German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel issued a tough statement on Sunday, demanding that Serbs loyal to Karadzic halt the wave of bombings against international monitors and NATO soldiers "immediately".
"It's outrageous that those who want to help are being attacked," Kinkel said two days after visiting Sarajevo.
British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook was expected to convey a similar message on Tuesday with leaders of the country's autonomous Moslem-Croat and Serb territories.

Countries sponsoring the 1995 Dayton peace treaty concluded that only arrest operations will succeed in bringing suspects to justice, said Duncan Bullivant, spokesman for the international High Representative to Bosnia.

Western powers met this month and "stood full square behind further operations, realising that physical arrests are now the only real option to getting these people off the scene," he told reporters on Monday.
A wave of low-level violence followed the NATO swoop on two Serbs charged with war crimes. No one has been killed but two U.S. soldiers and one Dutch soldier have been injured in explosions.
Serb hardliners grouped around ex-president Karadzic, who has been indicted twice by the tribunal, were stunned by the NATO raid and fear their grip on power is under serious threat.
Official Serb media have launched inflammatory attacks on the NATO-led peace force in Bosnia, accusing it of preparing manhunts against all men who served in the Bosnian Serb military.
Karadzic's allies are particularly disturbed at the existence of sealed, or secret indictments. They have repeatedly demanded Western diplomats tell them who has been charged by the tribunal.
"That's all they want to talk about," said one diplomat. "They are not quite as serene as they were."
Seventy-six people have been publicly indicted by the International Criminal Tribunal on former Yugoslavia, including Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb wartime military commander, General Ratko Mladic.

Western officials believe indictees responsible for carving up Bosnia in war through expulsions and murder of civilians must be removed from positions of influence and punished or there will be little hope of reintegrating the postwar ethnic sectors, repatriating refugees and reconciling Serb, Croat and Moslem communities.

More than two weeks since British soldiers seized one Serb suspect and shot dead another who resisted -- both had been indicted in secret -- speculation is raging across former Yugoslavia about who will be snatched next.
Balkan analysts said Washington might choose to allow a power struggle between Karadzic and his rival, Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic, to play itself out first before going after Karadzic.

The feud has already politically damaged Karadzic and thousands of people have attended rallies supporting Plavsic's campaign against corruption flourishing in part because of his alleged racketeering.

Western diplomats were also piling pressure on Croatian President Franjo Tudjman to deliver his wartime Bosnian Croat proteges under indictment, including Dario Kordic, former head of the Bosnian wing of Tudjman's nationalist Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ) party.
U.S. officials still hope that Tudjman, who is anxious to secure Croatia's membership in Western institutions, will eventually bow to the pressure and ensure the extradition of indicted Croats.
Most are believed to be holed up in Croat-controlled parts of Bosnia to which Croatian security forces have easy access, according to Western monitors.
Tudjman has repeatedly promised cooperation with the tribunal but contends that arrests are impossible if suspects are on Bosnian territory.
Major powers do not expect the patron of the Bosnian Serbs, Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic, to hand over Karadzic or other fugitives.
